subject: science
title: KS3 / Year 7-9 Science - Biology Environment
subtitle: Environment, ecosystems, pollution, climate change, carbon cycling, conservation, sustainability and environmental data skills.
description: A KS3 biology revision pack about environments and ecosystems. It covers key ecological terms, pollution, fertiliser run-off, bioaccumulation, weather and climate, the greenhouse effect, the carbon cycle, human impacts, recycling, conservation, sustainability and environmental investigation skills.

data.targetWord: the surroundings of an organism, including living and non-living things

examples.en-GB: An environment includes air, water, soil, sunlight, temperature and other organisms.

data.targetWord: a community of organisms interacting with each other and with the physical environment

examples.en-GB: A pond ecosystem includes living organisms as well as water, light, mud and oxygen.

data.targetWord: the place where an organism lives

examples.en-GB: A hedgerow can be a habitat for birds, insects and small mammals.

data.targetWord: all the organisms of one species living in an area

examples.en-GB: A rabbit population may increase if there is plenty of food and shelter.

data.targetWord: all the populations of different species living together in an area

examples.en-GB: A woodland community includes trees, fungi, insects, birds and mammals.

data.targetWord: the variety of living organisms in an area

examples.en-GB: A wildflower meadow usually has higher biodiversity than a closely mown lawn.

data.targetWord: organisms depending on each other and on their environment for survival

examples.en-GB: Bees depend on flowers for nectar, while many flowers depend on bees for pollination.

data.targetWord: a living part of an environment that can affect organisms

examples.en-GB: Predators, prey, food plants and diseases are biotic factors.

data.targetWord: a non-living part of an environment that can affect organisms

examples.en-GB: Light, water, oxygen, temperature and soil type are abiotic factors.

data.targetWord: the release of harmful substances or energy into the environment

examples.en-GB: Sewage entering a river is a form of water pollution.

data.targetWord: a harmful substance or form of energy released into the environment

examples.en-GB: Smoke contains pollutants that can irritate human lungs.

data.targetWord: pollution in the atmosphere, often from vehicles, fires, factories or power stations

examples.en-GB: Air pollution near a busy road can include nitrogen oxides and tiny particles.

data.targetWord: harmful substances entering water bodies such as rivers, ponds, lakes or seas

examples.en-GB: Fertilisers, sewage, oil and plastic can all cause water pollution.

data.targetWord: pollution that damages soil, habitats or land surfaces

examples.en-GB: Landfill, litter and chemical waste can cause land pollution.

data.targetWord: loud sound that disrupts organisms or human health

examples.en-GB: Noise from roads or airports can disturb feeding, communication and breeding.

data.targetWord: artificial light at night that disrupts behaviour or sleep patterns

examples.en-GB: Bright street lights can affect insects, bats and birds.

data.targetWord: fertiliser washed from fields into rivers or ponds by rain

examples.en-GB: Fertiliser run-off can add nitrates to water and cause rapid algae growth.

data.targetWord: mineral ions in fertilisers that help plants grow but can pollute water in high amounts

examples.en-GB: High nitrate concentration can lead to algae growth in rivers.

data.targetWord: rapid growth of algae, often caused by extra mineral ions in water

examples.en-GB: An algal bloom can block light and lead to lower oxygen levels.

data.targetWord: oxygen mixed into water that aquatic organisms need for respiration

examples.en-GB: Fish and invertebrates may die if dissolved oxygen becomes too low.

data.targetWord: a pollutant building up in organisms and becoming more concentrated along a food chain

examples.en-GB: A bird of prey may contain more pollutant than the small fish it eats.

data.targetWord: short-term atmospheric conditions such as temperature, rainfall, wind and sunshine

examples.en-GB: Rain today and wind tomorrow are examples of weather.

data.targetWord: the long-term pattern of weather in a region, measured over many years

examples.en-GB: Climate is based on long-term records rather than one hot or cold day.

data.targetWord: long-term changes in climate, including temperature, rainfall, storms and sea level

examples.en-GB: Climate change can shift habitats and affect food supply.

data.targetWord: the rise in Earth's average temperature

examples.en-GB: Global warming is one important part of climate change.

data.targetWord: a gas that absorbs some outgoing infrared radiation from Earth

examples.en-GB: Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour are greenhouse gases.

data.targetWord: the natural process where greenhouse gases keep Earth warm by trapping some heat

examples.en-GB: The natural greenhouse effect makes Earth warm enough for life.

data.targetWord: extra warming caused by increased greenhouse gases from human activity

examples.en-GB: Burning fossil fuels increases the enhanced greenhouse effect.

data.targetWord: heat radiation given out by Earth after its surface is warmed by sunlight

examples.en-GB: Greenhouse gases absorb some outgoing infrared radiation.

data.targetWord: the movement of carbon between the atmosphere, organisms, soil, oceans, rocks and fossil fuels

examples.en-GB: Photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition and combustion are processes in the carbon cycle.

data.targetWord: a place where carbon is held, such as the atmosphere, organisms, soil, oceans, rocks or fossil fuels

examples.en-GB: Coal is a long-term carbon store formed from ancient organisms.

data.targetWord: the process green plants and algae use to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water using light energy

examples.en-GB: Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

data.targetWord: the process by which cells release energy from glucose

examples.en-GB: Respiration produces carbon dioxide in many organisms.

data.targetWord: the breakdown of dead organisms and waste by decomposers

examples.en-GB: Decomposition returns carbon to soil and can add carbon dioxide to the air.

data.targetWord: burning a fuel in oxygen

examples.en-GB: Combustion of coal, oil or gas releases carbon dioxide.

data.targetWord: a non-renewable fuel formed from ancient organisms over millions of years

examples.en-GB: Coal, oil and natural gas are fossil fuels.

data.targetWord: clearing forests, often for farming, timber, roads, mining or settlements

examples.en-GB: Deforestation causes habitat loss and reduces photosynthesis.

data.targetWord: the growth of towns and cities

examples.en-GB: Urbanisation can cause habitat loss, air pollution, noise, light pollution and more surface run-off.

data.targetWord: processing used materials so they can be made into new products

examples.en-GB: Recycling aluminium can save energy compared with making aluminium from ore.

data.targetWord: an order of waste choices from best to worst, starting with reduce and ending with landfill

examples.en-GB: The waste hierarchy shows that reducing waste is usually better than recycling it.

data.targetWord: burying waste in the ground

examples.en-GB: Landfill is low in the waste hierarchy because it uses land and can produce methane.

data.targetWord: using resources in a way that meets current needs without making life harder for future generations

examples.en-GB: A sustainable school uses energy carefully and reduces waste.

data.targetWord: protecting species, habitats and ecosystems

examples.en-GB: A nature reserve is one method of conservation.

data.targetWord: a resource that can be replaced naturally on a human timescale if managed carefully

examples.en-GB: Wind, sunlight and sustainably managed forests are renewable resources.

data.targetWord: a resource used faster than it forms

examples.en-GB: Coal, oil, natural gas and many metal ores are non-renewable resources.

data.targetWord: a strip or link of habitat that lets organisms move between separate habitats

examples.en-GB: A wildlife corridor can help species find food, mates and shelter.

data.targetWord: a lichen species or lichen cover used as evidence about air quality

examples.en-GB: Some lichens are sensitive to air pollution, so fewer sensitive lichens may grow near busy roads.

data.targetWord: the factor changed or compared in an investigation

examples.en-GB: Fertiliser concentration is the independent variable in an algal growth investigation.

data.targetWord: the factor measured in an investigation

examples.en-GB: Algal growth is the dependent variable if fertiliser concentration is being tested.

data.targetWord: a factor kept the same so a test is fair

examples.en-GB: Light intensity, temperature and water volume can be control variables in an algae experiment.

data.title: Fertiliser Run-Off and Fish Deaths
data.instruction: Put the water pollution cause-effect chain in the correct order.
items: A farmer applies fertiliser containing nitrates to a field.
Heavy rain washes some fertiliser into a nearby river or pond.
Extra nitrates cause algae to grow rapidly.
Algae block light and then die.
Decomposers break down dead algae and use oxygen from the water.
Dissolved oxygen falls, so fish and invertebrates may die.

data.title: The Greenhouse Effect
data.instruction: Put the steps of the natural greenhouse effect in the correct order.
items: Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and reaches Earth.
Earth's surface absorbs energy and warms up.
The warm surface gives out infrared radiation.
Greenhouse gases absorb some outgoing infrared radiation.
Some heat is returned towards Earth, keeping the planet warm enough for life.

data.title: Carbon Moving Through a Simple Food Chain
data.instruction: Put the carbon movement steps in the correct order.
items: Carbon dioxide is present in the air.
Green plants use photosynthesis to make glucose containing carbon.
Animals eat plants, so carbon compounds move into animals.
Plants and animals respire, releasing carbon dioxide.
Dead organisms and waste are broken down by decomposers.
Decomposition can return carbon dioxide to the air and carbon compounds to soil.

data.title: Waste Hierarchy
data.instruction: Put the waste options from best to worst.
items: Reduce the amount of waste created.
Reuse items so they stay useful for longer.
Repair damaged items instead of replacing them.
Recycle materials into new products.
Recover energy from waste in a controlled plant.
Send mixed waste to landfill.
